title: Tu BiShvat, lived
hookLine: a fruit seder, or planting a tree
tomorrow: a book of the Bible that never names God. why read it aloud?

cards: Senior year, and the talk is all about leaving: which city, which school, who keeps the plants alive when you're gone. The Talmud tells of Honi, walking along a road, who sees a man planting a carob tree.
How long until it gives fruit? Seventy years, the man says. Honi asks the obvious question: and you're sure you'll live seventy years to eat from it?

teach.h: AS MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME.
teach.b: The man answers: I found this world with carob trees in it. As my ancestors planted for me, I plant for my children. That's the mood of Tu BiShvat.
The Mishnah calls it the new year for trees: the school of Hillel puts it on the fifteenth of Shevat, and Tu is fifteen written in Hebrew letters.
It falls in the middle of winter, when the sap is moving under the bark before anyone can see it. People keep the day in two ways.

teach.h: A FRUIT SEDER, OR A SEED.
teach.b: One is a fruit seder, a custom from the kabbalists: plates of fruit, some with hard shells, some with pits, some you can eat all the way through, each with its blessing, and cups of wine or juice.
The other is planting: a tree, a seed in a pot, herbs on a windowsill.

teach.h: PLANT FIRST, THEN GO GREET HIM.
teach.b: There's a saying from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: if you have a sapling in your hand and someone tells you the Messiah has come, plant the sapling first, then go out to greet him.
Planting doesn't wait for a perfect moment.
You plant now, for someone you may never meet. That's a good thing to do on the way out of a house, too.

how: On Tu BiShvat some families and communities hold a fruit seder with fruits, nuts and cups of wine or juice, and others plant trees or give money to plant them; eating a new fruit with its blessing is a common way to mark the day.

games.q: you're moving out in a few months. your little sister wants to start a garden with you this weekend. what does the carob story suggest?
o: start it now; plant for whoever comes after you.
wait; you won't be around to see it grow.
buy grown plants so you get to enjoy them first.
games.why: Honi's planter: I found the world with carob trees in it; as my ancestors planted for me, I plant for my children.

practice: For the sit, if there's a plant near you, touch one leaf or the soil and notice whether it's dry. If there's no plant, hold a piece of fruit and smell it.
Either way, bring to mind one thing you could plant or water this week, for someone who'll come after you.

wordCard.voice: Tu BiShvat: the fifteenth of Shevat, the new year for trees, kept with a plate of fruit or a seed in the ground.

orig.note: Hebrew: the fifteenth of Shevat; the letters tet and vav make fifteen.

carryVoice: Keep this one: plant something. As they planted for you, so you plant for whoever comes next.
